own_scenes.desc: El rap fue siempre, según David Toop, «habla sincopada sobre un ritmo funk». Con el sampler, a finales de los ochenta empezó el verdadero renacimiento del funk: hacia 1990 las grandes estrellas del rap sampleaban casi exclusivamente música de la Era Funk, y no la de Motown, el R&B anterior, el pop soul, el disco o el rock blanco. Los éxitos funk quedaron desguazados como un coche abandonado: «Turn This Mutha Out» de M. C. Hammer copia el coro de «Tear the Roof Off the Sucker», «U Can’t Touch This» repite el riff de «Super Freak» y Digital Underground usó «(Not Just) Knee Deep» en tres temas de Sons of the P. A la vez, raperos afrocéntricos recuperaban la conciencia negra de los sesenta. Las demandas legales lo han hecho más difícil, pero bajo el rap sigue el funk que lo engendró.

notes.text: En 1984 Afrika Bambaataa grabó «Unity» con James Brown. Desde 1986 el rap se llenó de samples suyos: Eric B. & Rakim con «I Know You Got Soul» (de Bobby Byrd), el grito de «Think (About It)» de Lyn Collins en «It Takes Two» de Rob Base y DJ E-Z Rock, «Funky Drummer» y «The Grunt» en «Rebel Without a Pause» de Public Enemy; en 1988 todo grupo de rap con contrato usaba a James Brown. Brown respondió en «I’m Real»: quitad mi voz «hasta que me paguéis».

notes.text: Desde 1987 el sampleo de funk fue el centro del rap; tras los pleitos (De La Soul contra los Turtles), en 1993 limpiar un sample era tan caro que los raperos volvieron a tocar con músicos.

refs.q: The legacy of the funk tradition can be found in the function of The Funk in modern rap music.
refs.para: The legacy of the funk tradition can be found in the function of The Funk in modern rap music. The modern incarnation of rap music was always understood to be, as rap writer David Toop put it, “syncopated speaking over a funk beat.” Mixing old records on turntables has always been an integral element of Hip Hop (rap) culture. However, with the advent of sampling technology, the ability to digitally “splice” pieces of older music into new tracks, the true revival of funk began in earnest. Since the late 1980s, rap music producers have used “samples” of older black music to enhance their beats. Around 1990, during the zenith of the sampling era, the most popular rap stars sampled Funk Era music almost exclusively, and without exception every original funk artist referred to in this book can be found reincarnated in some modern rap song. This cannot be said for Motown soul music artists, earlier rhythm and blues artists, pop soul artists, disco artists, or mainstream (i.e. white) rock artists.
refs.chapter: Cap. 1: Introducción al funk: The Bomb

refs.q: Most of the “greatest hits” of the Funk Era have been stripped of all usable parts like an abandoned car.
refs.para: Rather than loop music from out of the tradition, rap samplers are uncanny in their integrity about the records they choose to pillage. Most of the “greatest hits” of the Funk Era have been stripped of all usable parts like an abandoned car. Vibe magazine called James Brown’s 1974 recording of “The Payback” as the sample of the year for 1992, naming a half dozen raps that use the old loop. Rap superstar M. C. Hammer’s first national hit, “Turn This Mutha Out,” featured a chant that was taken verbatim from the chorus of Parliament’s 1975 number-one soul hit, “Tear the Roof Off the Sucker.” Hammer’s biggest hit ever, “You Can’t Touch This,” used the basic riff from Rick James’ 1981 hit “Super Freak” repeated endlessly. The rap group Digital Underground looped the number-one 1979 Funkadelic single “(Not Just) Knee Deep” on three separate songs of their 1991 gold record LP, Sons of the P, and it goes on and on.
refs.chapter: Cap. 1: Introducción al funk: The Bomb

refs.q: By 1988, literally every rap act with a contract recorded James Brown samples on their records.
refs.para: By 1985 Brown was enjoying a worldwide renaissance as a result of “Living in America,” a worldwide smash hit. Yet this pop phenomenon had little to do with what was happening in da hood. By 1986 rap acts were starting to capture James Brown riffs in selected samples of his older music. New York rap group Eric B. & Rakim produced a version of “I Know You Got Soul,” one of many James Brown–produced songs (this one cut by Bobby Byrd in 1971). The record was a huge club hit and Brown was given no credit on the cover. The popular 1988 dance hit “It Takes Two” by Rob Base and DJ Easy Rock featured a catchy squeal-and-yell gimmick that was sequenced onto every beat, as a percussion effect throughout the song, without break. The sounds were unmistakably James Brown–era samples, and the record had an electrifying, breathless quality to it (the loop was a yelp from Lyn Collins’s James Brown–produced “Think [About It]”). Long Island hard-core rappers Public Enemy blew onto the scene with a wicked twelve-inch single “Rebel Without a Pause,” also in the summer of 1987—a track that looped the 1970 James Brown instrumental “The Funky Drummer” as a drum track, and scorched the highs with a repeating Maceo Parker saxophone screech from the 1972 JBs instrumental “The Grunt.” The record was a club monster, and it was clear that there could be more where this came from. The James Brown sound was out of the bag, and James Brown was it. By 1988, literally every rap act with a contract recorded James Brown samples on their records.

podcast.title: Advanced Concepts (1983)
podcast.body: Highly advanced concepts of sampling were evident in tracks such as West Street Mob's "Break Dance - Electric Boogie" in 1983, marking a significant evolution towards mid-80s hip hop. "tiene conceptos avanzadísimos lo que es el sampling el break beat es una pizza avanzadísima de lo que luego sería el hip hop de mitad de los 80."

podcast.title: Integration into Hip Hop (1984)
podcast.body: By 1984, sampling was fully integrated into what was considered hip hop culture, as seen in releases like Crash Crew's "Breaking Bells." "la mayoría la gran mayoría de lanzamientos de rap encaja muy bien dentro de lo que consideramos la cultura hip hop la cultura del break beat la cultura del sampling."
